title: Can Israel End Its Forever Wars?
gist: Haaretz defense analyst Amos Harel argues that centrist challenger Gadi Eisenkot, who leads Netanyahu in Israeli polls ahead of the October 27, 2026 election, would likely bring only incremental (not dramatic) change to Israeli security policy -- restraining West Bank settler violence and seeking to wind down fronts in Gaza, Lebanon, and Syria -- with the scope of change hinging heavily on Eisenkot's ability to build personal rapport with Trump, given Israel has already spent roughly $142 billion (over half its annual budget) on the war since October 7.

themes.theme: Netanyahu's 'continuous war' doctrine and its costs

insights.claim: Netanyahu has adopted an explicit strategy of waging wars without end, arguing Israel must take preemptive military action against every potential security threat regardless of consequences, as a lesson drawn from Hamas's October 7, 2023 attack.
insights.speaker: Amos Harel
insights.so_what: Establishes the core policy baseline (permanent preemptive war) against which any change of government would be measured -- a key variable for regional conflict-risk and defense-spending forecasts.
insights.quote: He now publicly and explicitly supports waging wars without end. As a lesson of Hamas's October 7, 2023, massacre, he asserts that Israel needs to take preemptive military action against every potential security threat it faces, regardless of the consequences.

insights.claim: Israel has spent about $142 billion on the war since it began in October 2023, equivalent to more than half of the country's total annual budget, alongside reservists serving on average more than 100 days a year and no time for the IDF to train.
insights.speaker: Amos Harel
insights.so_what: A hard fiscal data point ($142B, >50% of annual budget) quantifying war-driven fiscal strain on Israel -- directly relevant to sovereign-risk assessment, Israeli bond/shekel outlook, and defense-budget allocation forecasts.
insights.quote: Israel has spent about $142 billion on the war since it began—equivalent to more than half of the country's total annual budget.
insights.locator: paragraph on the cost of Netanyahu's strategy

insights.claim: Israeli cabinet members including Defense Minister Israel Katz are searching for new military foes, casting Turkish President Erdogan as a threat comparable to Hezbollah and Hamas, and some ministers claim without evidence that Syria's president Ahmed al-Shara is preparing to attack Israel.
insights.speaker: Amos Harel
insights.so_what: Flags unsubstantiated threat-inflation by Israeli cabinet officials against Turkey and Syria's new government -- a risk indicator for potential unnecessary escalation independent of actual security threats.
insights.quote: Some of these cabinet members have even maintained, without a shred of evidence, that Syria's president, the former jihadist Ahmed al-Shara, is preparing to attack Israel.

insights.claim: Gadi Eisenkot, a former IDF chief of staff running as leader of the new Yashar party, has opened a substantial lead over Netanyahu in polls ahead of the October 27, 2026 election, driven partly by defections of traditional Likud voters.
insights.speaker: Amos Harel
insights.so_what: A concrete, dated electoral signpost (Oct 27, 2026 election) with a specific frontrunner (Eisenkot) -- a key event for geopolitical-risk calendars tracking Israeli policy continuity/discontinuity.
insights.quote: In recent polls, Yashar has taken a lead over Likud, and Eisenkot has opened a substantial gap over Netanyahu on a key question: suitability to serve as prime minister.

insights.claim: Despite leading in polls, Eisenkot has been deliberately vague on national security strategy and has stated opposition to a Palestinian state -- a position that is now consensus across Israel's political center and parts of the center-left as well as the right.
insights.speaker: Amos Harel
insights.so_what: Signals that even a change of government in Israel would not restore a two-state framework as a live policy option -- important baseline for anyone modeling a durable Israeli-Palestinian settlement scenario.
insights.quote: In a rare statement on such matters in August, Eisenkot said he was opposed to a Palestinian state, endorsing what is by now a consensus position across Israel's political center.

insights.claim: Harel's central thesis is that an Eisenkot government would bring real but incremental, not dramatic, policy shifts on the West Bank, Syria, and Gaza -- explicitly rejecting the view that there would be no meaningful difference from Netanyahu.
insights.speaker: Amos Harel
insights.so_what: Sets investor/analyst expectations correctly: a post-Netanyahu Israel is not a regime-change scenario for markets or regional stability, but a moderation-at-the-margins scenario.
insights.quote: There are a number of important areas... where new strategies could yield real dividends, even if the changes are most likely to be incremental rather than dramatic.

insights.claim: Eisenkot's political mission was catalyzed by personal tragedy: his son Gal, a reservist, was killed in December 2023 in an operation to recover hostage remains in Gaza, after which Eisenkot publicly pledged accountability for the security failures behind October 7.
insights.speaker: Amos Harel
insights.so_what: Provides personal-motivation context that helps explain Eisenkot's political durability and public trust, relevant to assessing the authenticity/staying-power of his political brand versus a purely opportunistic challenge.
insights.quote: In an emotional eulogy at his son's funeral, Eisenkot pledged to work to repair the flaws exposed in Israeli society: to answer the public demand for accountability.

themes.theme: West Bank settler violence and institutional capture

insights.claim: Since 2023, more than 200 new Israeli settlements and outposts have been built or are under construction in the West Bank under Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, in some cases displacing original Palestinian landowners, with Netanyahu giving Smotrich a free hand over civilian affairs there.
insights.speaker: Amos Harel
insights.so_what: A hard, countable data point (200+ new settlements since 2023) documenting the scale of West Bank land-control expansion under the current government -- material to assessing the durability of any future two-state option.
insights.quote: Since 2023, more than 200 new settlements and outposts have been built or are under construction.

insights.claim: The settler movement now combines a political arm (ministers, Knesset members, regional council heads) with an increasingly powerful, well-armed military arm of close to 1,000 mostly young settlers, whose weapons access has expanded since 2023 under National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.
insights.speaker: Amos Harel
insights.so_what: Describes an institutionalizing armed non-state actor (nearly 1,000-strong, government-enabled) operating with growing autonomy from formal IDF/police command -- a rising instability risk for the West Bank distinct from the Gaza conflict.
insights.quote: The military one is now a violent group of close to 1,000 mostly young settlers... This cohort is increasingly well armed: Israel's far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, has expanded settlers' access to guns and weapons since 2023.

insights.claim: Harel argues settlers and their political allies are jointly pursuing what in its most extreme form amounts to localized ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, with the army and police wary of confronting violent settlers who act with impunity.
insights.speaker: Amos Harel
insights.so_what: A striking, explicit characterization from a mainstream Israeli defense analyst (not an outside critic) -- signals the severity of the West Bank breakdown is now being named plainly within Israel's own defense-commentary establishment.
insights.quote: In reality, however, they are all working toward the same goal: seizure of land and expulsion, which in its most extreme form amounts to localized ethnic cleansing.

insights.claim: It has been more than 20 years since the last large-scale evacuation of Israeli settlers (the removal of nearly 9,000 from Gaza in 2005 under Ariel Sharon), and many IDF officers now identify with settlers and religious-right parties, meaning any future evacuation order could face broad noncompliance.
insights.speaker: Amos Harel
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific institutional-loyalty risk (IDF officer sympathy with settlers) that would constrain even a reform-minded government's ability to reverse West Bank settlement expansion -- a durable structural constraint, not just a political one.
insights.quote: Given how many IDF officers and soldiers now identify with the settlers and the religious-right parties, any order to evacuate even a handful of settlements could lead to broad noncompliance.

insights.claim: Netanyahu has appointed officers seen as personally loyal or ideologically aligned with settlers to Israel's top security posts, including his own military secretary Major General Roman Gofman as Mossad chief and hawkish religious officer Major General David Zini as Shin Bet chief.
insights.speaker: Amos Harel
insights.so_what: Documents specific personnel evidence of politicization within Israel's top intelligence services, relevant to assessing institutional independence and future policy continuity risk even after a change in government.
insights.quote: Particularly notable was the prime minister's decision to appoint an officer he described as “discreet and loyal”—his military secretary, Major General Roman Gofman—as head of the Mossad.

themes.theme: Regional diplomacy: Gaza, Lebanon, Syria, and the Trump factor

insights.claim: Unlike Netanyahu, Eisenkot never promised 'total victory' over Hamas and has publicly criticized Netanyahu for promoting illusions about what could be achieved, suggesting he would have more room to accept a reduced Israeli zone of control in Gaza alongside internationally supervised Palestinian Authority involvement elsewhere in the strip.
insights.speaker: Amos Harel
insights.so_what: Outlines the most plausible endgame scenario for Gaza under a new Israeli government -- partial Israeli withdrawal plus PA-administered zones -- a scenario relevant to reconstruction-investment and regional-stability planning.
insights.quote: The most plausible best-case scenario, then, would be a reduced but still significant Israeli zone of control in Gaza, accompanied by stepwise plans for some kind of internationally supervised PA involvement in the unoccupied half.

insights.claim: Syria's president Ahmed al-Shara is reportedly interested in a security arrangement involving Israeli withdrawal from territory captured from Syria in 2024 in exchange for partial normalization of relations, which Harel says Eisenkot could view as a reasonable, low-risk provisional arrangement.
insights.speaker: Amos Harel
insights.so_what: Flags a concrete, near-term Israel-Syria normalization opportunity contingent on Israeli leadership change -- a specific diplomatic development to monitor for signs of a broader regional realignment.
insights.quote: Shara is interested in reaching a security arrangement that would include an Israeli withdrawal from territories captured from Syria in 2024 in exchange for partial normalization of relations.

insights.claim: Harel argues Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman might be more disposed toward normalization talks with an Eisenkot government, viewing it as a break from Israel's 'toxic right-wing leadership.'
insights.speaker: Amos Harel
insights.so_what: Suggests a change in Israeli leadership could unlock Saudi-Israel normalization talks, a scenario with significant implications for Gulf-Israel relations and regional energy/security diplomacy.
insights.quote: It's also possible that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman would regard an Eisenkot government as turning a page from Israel's toxic right-wing leadership and be more disposed to begin negotiations toward normalization.

insights.claim: The U.S. is entangled in an Iran war that has already lasted almost six months, contradicting Trump's own stated preferences, and Trump has periodically blamed Netanyahu for the war's failure while rejecting Netanyahu's pleas to escalate against Tehran.
insights.speaker: Amos Harel
insights.so_what: Confirms an active, prolonged (~6-month) U.S.-Iran military conflict as of publication, a major and ongoing geopolitical/oil-market risk factor that should be a headline input for macro and energy risk assessments.
insights.quote: The U.S. administration is entangled in a war in Iran that has already lasted almost six months, in complete contradiction of everything Trump preached for years.

insights.claim: Harel argues that how much Israeli policy actually changes under a new government depends heavily on the personal rapport between Israel's next prime minister and Trump, noting Eisenkot lacks Netanyahu's diplomatic experience, fluent American English, and personal charisma with Trump.
insights.speaker: Amos Harel
insights.so_what: Identifies personal chemistry with Trump -- not institutional policy -- as the pivotal variable determining whether Israeli strategy actually shifts, a soft but consequential geopolitical risk factor that is hard to model quantitatively.
insights.quote: A great deal hinges on whether the new prime minister can find some chemistry with the U.S. president.
